Proponents argued this approach supplied an empirical foundation for viewing cognitive differences as stable and population-specific rather than situational. A claimed advantage was that observed gaps in literacy, invention, or state-building could be assigned to biology instead of conquest, forced migration, or exclusion from schooling.

Generalized portraits of behavior drew from accounts of plantation labor, trading posts, and colonial expeditions. Common descriptions included claims that populations south of the Sahara exhibited limited capacity for long-term planning, lower impulse control in certain contexts, or primary orientation toward concrete rather than symbolic tasks. Selective chronologies focused on the absence of widespread alphabetic literacy or certain forms of monumental architecture in many interior African societies before sustained European contact, while minimizing or omitting West African states that produced extensive trade networks, cavalry forces, and urban centers (Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Great Zimbabwe). Introduction

Biological Inferiority

One of the most prominent pseudoscientific theories regarding the inferiority of Black people is the concept of "scientific racism." This theory, popularized by figures like Louis Agassiz and Samuel Morton, argues that Black people are biologically inferior to other races, particularly Caucasians. The intellectual inferiority of Black people is often supported by the stereotype of the "lazy Negro."
